body.heading: A dense centre and a lot of empty space
paragraphs: An atom has two regions. At the centre sits the nucleus, a tight knot of particles that holds almost all of the atom's mass. Moving around the nucleus are electrons, each carrying a small negative electric charge. The nucleus carries a matching positive charge, so a complete atom is electrically neutral overall.

The surprising part is the emptiness. If an atom were enlarged to the size of a football stadium, its nucleus would be about the size of a marble at the centre. Everything else is space, with the electrons spread through it. Solid objects feel solid not because atoms are solid, but because of the forces between them.

body.heading: Three particles that explain chemistry
paragraphs: Protons sit in the nucleus with a positive charge, and their number is the atom's identity card: every atom with one proton is hydrogen, every atom with six is carbon, and so on through all the elements. Change the proton count and you have changed the element itself.

Neutrons share the nucleus but carry no charge; they add mass and hold the nucleus together, and atoms of the same element can carry different numbers of them — these variants are called isotopes. Electrons are far lighter than either and are the particles that get shared, swapped and shuffled whenever atoms join or react, which is why chemistry is mostly the story of electrons.

body.heading: How small is an atom, really?
paragraphs: Atoms are measured in tenths of a nanometre — a nanometre being a billionth of a metre. Roughly a million atoms side by side would span the width of a single human hair, and no ordinary microscope can show you one; scientists image them with instruments that feel their way across a surface atom by atom.

Small as they are, they add up. Your body contains around seven thousand trillion trillion atoms, the great majority of them hydrogen, oxygen and carbon. Every one of them was once forged inside a star or in the violence just after the universe began.

description: Every object you have ever touched is built from atoms — tiny particles with a dense centre and electrons in motion around it.
